head:
Health · Strength

What push-ups say about your heart

How many push-ups can you do in a row? A figure that circulates says that managing more than 40 push-ups would cut your heart risk twenty-five-fold. This article goes back to the study it comes from, reads it in detail, places it among the other studies on strength, and says what can be taken from it without fooling yourself.

The problem

The starting point is a press headline from February 2019. Researchers from Harvard and Indiana University published in JAMA Network Open the follow-up of 1,104 male firefighters, tested once on push-ups and then followed for about ten years.1,3 The result picked up everywhere: those who did more than 40 push-ups had 96% fewer cardiovascular events than those who did 10 or fewer.3 The figure is spectacular, it is simple, and it appears word for word on many fitness advice pages.

A figure this clear-cut deserves to be checked before it is quoted. Where exactly does it come from? How many events are behind it? In which people? And above all, what does it mean for someone who is neither a firefighter nor a 40-year-old man? The "96%" comes from a test that takes two minutes and costs nothing, which makes it appealing. That is also what forces us to ask whether it really measures what we think it measures.

The question splits in two. The first is descriptive: does the number of push-ups a person can do tell you anything about their risk of a heart problem? The second is a question about action: if so, is it because the strength of the arms and trunk protects the heart, or because this test reveals something else, such as general fitness, weight, lifestyle or the absence of a silent disease? In the first case, the test is a thermometer. In the second, working on push-ups would already be a lever. You cannot go from one to the other without evidence.

The question

Does the number of push-ups you can do say anything about the health of your heart, and if so, how far can you rely on it: for you, for a woman, for someone who does not have the profile of the firefighters in the study?

We answer in six steps, from the broadest to the most precise: hand strength in hundreds of thousands of people, the comparison with other tests, a follow-up of men that separates strength from endurance, the push-up study itself, what limits its conclusions, and then what is not yet known.

What is at stake

Cardiovascular diseases are the leading cause of death in the United States, for men and for women alike, and the firefighter study starts from that observation.1 In the profession studied, heart risk is particularly present: a physician quoted by a health website points out that firefighting is a job known for high rates of cardiac deaths.4 This is not a detail, as we will see, because it defines the ground on which the result was obtained.

What is at stake for you is concrete. A cardiac event (heart failure, sudden death, a diagnosis of coronary artery disease) is often the first visible sign of a problem that has been building for years. The usual tools to anticipate it are blood pressure, cholesterol, smoking, weight. They require a blood test, an appointment, equipment. A test you can do in your living room, with nobody else around, changes the balance of power: you can place yourself, repeat it, see whether you are improving.

What is also at stake is the false sense of security. A high push-up score replaces neither a check-up nor a consultation for chest pain. And a low score is not a sentence. A simple test is only useful if you know precisely what it predicts, for whom, and with what margin of error. That is what this demonstration sets out to establish.

Finally, there is the training question. If upper-body strength is an independent health marker, it deserves a real place in a programme, alongside cardio. If it is only a reflection, the priority lies elsewhere. Better to know before deciding how to split your sessions.
rest:
Step 1 of 6 · The whole population

In hundreds of thousands of people, hand strength predicts mortality

Before looking at push-ups, we need to know whether upper-body muscular strength says anything in general. The best-studied test is grip strength, measured by squeezing a dynamometer. It requires no technique and is easy to standardise, which explains the number of studies.

The largest is PURE: 139,691 adults aged 35 to 70 in 17 countries with very different incomes, including 58,652 men and 81,039 women, followed for about 4 years, during which 3,379 died.6,7 For each 5 kg drop in hand strength, the risk of all-cause death is 16% higher, that of cardiovascular death 17%, that of heart attack 7% and that of stroke 9%.6

The weaker the grip, the higher the risk of death, including from cardiac causes

Adjusted risk ratios per 5 kg drop in grip strength, converted to percentages (1.16 becomes +16%). Source: Leong et al., PURE, The Lancet, 2015, from two reports.6,7

What this means

5 kg is the gap between two people of the same age and sex, one of whom squeezes slightly less hard. This modest gap corresponds to a risk of death that is 16% higher. The same report notes that grip strength predicted mortality better than systolic blood pressure in this cohort, which the authors present as an exploratory analysis.6 For you: a very simple strength measurement carries information about your future health, including your heart.

A second, British cohort confirms it. In the UK Biobank, 502,293 people aged 40 to 69 (54% women) were followed for 7.1 years on average, with 13,322 deaths. For each 5 kg drop in hand strength, the risk of dying from any cause is 1.20 times higher in women and 1.16 times in men. For cardiovascular deaths, 1.19 in women and 1.22 in men.8 The signal is of the same order in both sexes. One result remains open: these authors note that the value of grip strength within a risk score remains to be established.8

This is a first step. It remains to be checked that it is not an artefact of one test or one country, and to see whether strength tells more than other simple measures.

Step 2 of 6 · The other tests, both sexes

Strength is not the only measure that predicts, but it also predicts in women

A British meta-analysis gathered 28 articles on simple physical tests done in the general population, followed until death.9 It compares the weakest quarter with the strongest quarter on each test. For hand strength: 14 studies, 53,476 people, a risk of death 1.67 times higher. For the timed chair rise: 1.96, across 5 studies. For walking speed: 2.87, across 5 studies.9

Several simple physical tests separate the survivors from the others, including in women

Risk ratios for all-cause death, weakest quarter versus strongest quarter. Adjustment limited to age, sex and body size. Source: Cooper et al., BMJ, 2010.9

What this means

A ratio of 1.67 means that, over the course of the studies, people in the weakest quarter died about two-thirds more often than those in the strongest quarter. Walking and chair rise predict even more, but almost all of these studies involved people over 70.9 Hand strength is the only one of the three measures well documented in younger adults, and even there the figure drops (1.43 in people under 60, across only five studies).9

The breakdown by sex for hand strength gives 1.75 in men and 1.46 in women. The gap exists and stays in the same direction: in women too, a weak hand goes with a higher risk of death.9 The authors add that the heterogeneity between studies is high for grip strength, which means that the figure of 1.67 is an order of magnitude and not a constant.9

So we have a broad, consistent signal. But it concerns mortality, not cardiac events specifically, and it concerns grip strength. To know whether overall muscular strength adds anything to endurance, we need a follow-up that measures both.

Step 3 of 6 · Strength or endurance?

In men followed for 19 years, a higher level of strength goes with fewer deaths, mainly when leaving the bottom of the ranking

The Cooper Clinic cohort in Dallas followed 8,762 men for 18.9 years on average (165,251 person-years): 503 deaths, 145 of them of cardiovascular origin.10 The men are divided into three thirds according to their muscular strength. Death rates per 10,000 person-years, adjusted for age, are 38.9 for the weakest third, 25.9 for the middle third and 26.6 for the strongest third.10

The biggest gap is between the least strong men and the others

Death rates per 10,000 person-years, adjusted for age, by third of muscular strength. Source: Ruiz et al., BMJ, 2008.10

What this means

Going from the weakest third to the middle third comes with a large drop in the death rate (from 38.9 to 25.9). Going from the middle to the strongest changes almost nothing (26.6). After adjustment for physical activity, smoking, alcohol, BMI and history, the risk of all-cause death is 0.72 times that of the weak third for the middle third and 0.77 for the strong third.10 For you: most of the advantage comes from leaving the bottom of the ranking, not from chasing the top.

Cardiovascular mortality follows the same slope (12.1, 7.6 and 6.6 per 10,000 person-years), with an adjusted risk ratio of 0.74 and 0.71, but these two ratios are not statistically significant: their confidence intervals go down to 0.50 and 0.47 and up to 1.10 and 1.07.10 And here is the detail that matters for our question: when the authors add endurance (cardiorespiratory fitness) to the calculation, the link between strength and cardiovascular death stops being significant, whereas the link with all-cause mortality and with cancer mortality persists.10

This is a first clue that, for the heart, part of what strength "predicts" is already carried by endurance. This cohort also has limits that the authors point out: men who were mostly white, from affluent and educated backgrounds, who came for a medical visit, and no women because deaths were too rare.10 Another follow-up, from Finland, shows that hand strength also goes with heart rhythm: among 827 adults aged about 69 followed for nearly 16 years, there were 265 cases of atrial fibrillation, with a risk 25% lower for moderate strength and 39% lower for high strength, compared with the weak group.15

We now have enough context to look at the push-up study itself, with its real figures.

Step 4 of 6 · Push-ups

The firefighter study: what it measured, and the figure that comes out of it

Here is the protocol as the sources describe it. Indiana firefighters, recruited from 10 departments, had annual examinations between 2000 and 2010.1,4 At baseline, they did as many push-ups as possible while following a metronome set at 80; the test stopped at 80 push-ups, at giving up, or after three missed beats.4 They also did a submaximal treadmill test.1,3 More than 1,500 men were included (1,562 according to one report) and 1,104 were analysed, for 8,601 person-years of follow-up.2,4 I did not find the reason for this gap.

Push-ups were grouped into five categories: 0 to 10, 11 to 20, 21 to 30, 31 to 40 and more than 40.1 The mean age was 39.6 years, the mean BMI 28.7 (overweight).3 The follow-up recorded 37 cardiovascular events (heart failure, sudden cardiac death or diagnosis of coronary artery disease, according to a press report).1,5 All but one occurred in men who had done 40 push-ups or fewer at baseline.3

The incidence rate ratio for more than 40 push-ups, compared with the weakest group, is 0.04, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.01 to 0.36.2,1 Hence the "96%": 1 minus 0.04.

The "96%" is a central estimate; the plausible range is very wide

Incidence rate ratio (more than 40 push-ups versus the weakest group), estimate and 95% confidence interval. Logarithmic scale: each tick multiplies by 10. Source: Yang et al., JAMA Network Open, 2019, from reports of the study.2,1

What this means

The thick line is the zone of values compatible with the data. It runs from 0.01 to 0.36. Translated into risk reduction (derived calculation, 1 minus the bound): from 64% to 99%. It is not "96%" that should be remembered but "very probably a large reduction, whose exact size is uncertain". The uncertainty is wide because there are only 37 events in total, and just one among those with more than 40 push-ups.

One point must be flagged honestly: not all reports give the same value. The Cooper Institute post speaks, after adjustment for age and BMI, of a reduction of "nearly 90%" for more than 40 push-ups, whereas the Harvard press release and the others give 96%.1,3 I could not read the table of the original paper, which would settle it. In both cases the qualitative conclusion is the same, but the "-96%" should not be quoted as a constant.

One last result to keep in mind: the authors write that push-up capacity was more strongly associated with cardiovascular events than performance on the submaximal treadmill test.1,3 No figure is given in the reports I read for this comparison. It is surprising, since step 3 suggested that endurance carries most of the cardiac information. A submaximal test estimates endurance roughly, and that may be the reason, but I cannot assert it.

So this result stands, but it still has to be examined closely: who are these men, how many events, and what alternative explanations?

Step 5 of 6 · The objections

Why we cannot say "40 push-ups protect the heart"

A single profession, middle-aged men

All the participants are active male firefighters, around 40 years old. The authors themselves write that the result cannot be generalised to women, to men of other ages or to less active people.1,3 A serving firefighter has passed fitness criteria at hiring, which selects people who are rather healthy, a classic selection bias. In another firefighter study, researchers also point out that the performance thresholds used in this job were set without validated norms for this population.16

Very few events

With 37 events, a few more or fewer cases would shift the result strongly, as the interval of 0.01 to 0.36 shows. And these 37 are spread over five push-up categories, which leaves each with a tiny number. The reports I read do not give these numbers by group, except for the last one: a single event among those with more than 40 push-ups.3

The test measures something other than the arms

Doing many push-ups depends on strength, but also on muscular endurance, body weight and technique. During a full push-up, the arms carry about 69% of body weight at the top and 75% at the bottom, according to a study of 28 people relayed by the Cooper Institute.14 At equal strength, a heavier person therefore does fewer. BMI was taken into account in the adjustment, which limits the problem without removing it.1

Risk factors go with the score

In this study, the men who did the most push-ups also had better risk factors: less smoking, lower blood pressure.1 Part of the observed gap may therefore come from these factors rather than from push-ups. The authors do not claim, moreover, that push-ups are an independent risk factor.1 Ruiz and colleagues reach a similar conclusion for the Dallas cohort: the link between strength and cardiovascular death disappears once endurance is taken into account.10

Reverse causation

Someone who is coming down with a disease may do fewer push-ups before even knowing they are ill. In that case, it is not weakness that prepares the event, it is the onset of the disease that weakens. The authors of the Dallas cohort judge this scenario less likely in their case, but do not rule it out, like any observational study.10 For the firefighters, men in active service with no restrictions, it is plausible that this bias is reduced, though the sources I read do not demonstrate it.

What this means

The objections do not destroy the result, they change its status: a strong but imprecise association, observed in a narrow profile, which may partly reflect general fitness, smoking or blood pressure. That is enough to say that push-ups are an interesting indicator. It is not enough to promise that your push-up score changes your heart risk.

It remains to look at what, in the literature, goes beyond observation: whether strengthening your muscles lowers the risk.

Step 6 of 6 · What remains uncertain

Does training strength help, and what about women?

None of the studies I read shows that increasing your number of push-ups reduces cardiac events. That would take a randomised trial: one group trained on push-ups, one group that is not, and a follow-up over years. I did not find one.

What we have are meta-analyses of cohorts on strength training. The one by Momma and colleagues (16 studies, up to 25 years of follow-up) concludes a 15% lower risk of all-cause mortality and a 17% lower risk of cardiovascular events for those who do strength training, with a maximum benefit at around 40 minutes per week for mortality and 60 minutes for cardiovascular disease, and a benefit that then diminishes (J-shaped curve for the heart).11 Another meta-analysis (10 studies, ages 18 to 85, 7 to 17 years of follow-up) gives 15% lower all-cause mortality and 19% lower cardiovascular mortality, with 26% lower for about 60 minutes per week.12 The same source indicates that combining strength training with moderate-to-vigorous activity goes with 40% lower mortality, against 18% for strength training alone and 25% for aerobic activity alone.12

What this means

These figures are associations between reported habits and mortality, not measured effects of a programme. In the meta-analysis of source 12, activity was reported by questionnaire, and the reports I read give no confidence intervals for either one.11,12 Their interest lies elsewhere: they all point the same way, and the best result comes from the combination of strength plus endurance, not from strength alone.

For women, the picture is thinner. The push-up study included only men, and so did the Dallas cohort. I did not find a study that directly links the number of push-ups in women to their cardiac events. What we have is indirect: hand strength predicts mortality in women, with ratios of 1.20 in the UK Biobank and 1.46 in the 2010 meta-analysis.8,9 Nothing says that the "40 push-ups" threshold applies to a woman, and since the full push-up is harder at equal weight for most women, it would be misleading to apply it to them.

The answer to the question

Let us go back to the question: does the number of push-ups you can do say anything about the health of your heart?

What is solid. Upper-body muscular strength, measured at the hand, goes with mortality and cardiovascular events in several very large cohorts (PURE, UK Biobank, the 2010 meta-analysis), in men and in women. The biggest gap is seen between the weakest and the others.

What is probable. Push-ups take part in this signal. In the Indiana firefighters, the difference is considerable, but it rests on 37 events in a single profession, with a range that goes from 64% to 99% reduction. For an active man of about 40, doing fewer than 10 push-ups is probably a warning sign, and doing more than 40 is probably a good sign. Probably, not certainly.

What is not established. That push-ups protect the heart by themselves, that the threshold of 40 holds for women, for older or younger people, or that gaining push-ups reduces risk. The "-96%" is not a figure to promise anyone. On causality, the data I read point rather towards a marker of general fitness (mainly endurance, step 3), with perhaps a part specific to strength.

What to put in place

The push-up test is a personal benchmark, repeated under the same conditions, not a diagnosis. Here is how to use it.

  1. Do the test with the same protocol every time.In the study, a metronome set at 80 gave the pace, and the test stopped at 80 push-ups, at giving up or after three missed beats.4 Use the tempo and the execution instructions (hand and foot position, alignment, range of motion) from the THW test page, and keep the same variant: the knee push-up carries only 54 to 62% of body weight against 69 to 75% for the full one, so the two cannot be compared.14
  2. Compare yourself with yourself, not with the figure of 40.No validated norm table links a number of push-ups to a heart risk outside this cohort of firefighters. Note your score, then redo it every 6 to 8 weeks (a follow-up rhythm suggested here, not drawn from any study). If the score drops for no clear reason or you are short of breath, talk to someone about it.
  3. Work on strength and endurance together.The combination of strength training and aerobic activity is associated with the largest drop in mortality (40%, against 18% and 25% for each alone).12 The dose associated with the best result is of the order of 40 to 60 minutes of strength training per week.11,12 These are associations, not a promise.
  4. If you have a dynamometer, measure your hand too.Median grip strength values in Great Britain give a benchmark (figure below). For a 40-year-old man, the median is 50 kg; for a woman of the same age, 31 kg.13 Measurement protocols vary from one study to another, so the comparison is approximate.

Hand strength falls slowly until 60, then drops

Median grip strength by age, general British population (12 studies, 49,964 people), men and women. Values at the nearest tabulated ages. Source: Dodds et al., PLoS ONE, 2014.13

What this means

Between 25 and 45, the median stays stable (around 48 to 51 kg in men, 30 to 31 kg in women), then declines: 45 kg at 60 in men, 32 kg at 80, 29 kg at 85. For you, losing strength with age is the norm, but the pace is not fixed: it is an argument to measure and train before the slope steepens.13

A full push-up carries clearly more weight than a knee push-up

Share of body weight carried by the upper body by variant. Study of 28 people (Suprak et al., 2011), from the Cooper Institute: small sample, indicative values.14

A very low score, chest pain, unusual shortness of breath, feeling faint during effort: see a doctor before testing yourself or training harder. The push-up test replaces neither a check-up nor a doctor's advice.

What these figures do not say
  • The push-up study covers 1,104 active male firefighters of about 40, with 37 events; it does not apply as it stands to women, to other ages or to other profiles.1,3
  • All the relationships come from observational studies. No trial I read shows that increasing your number of push-ups reduces cardiac events.
  • The exact values of the original paper (tables by category, adjustments) could not be read: the figures come from reports, which diverge between 90% and 96%.1,2,3

Frequently asked questions

Should I aim for 40 push-ups?

This threshold comes from a category in the study (more than 40), not from a health norm table. It was only observed in male firefighters, and nothing says it holds for you.1,3

I can only do 10 push-ups, should I worry?

A low score is a signal to train and, if you have other reasons to be concerned, to talk to a doctor. It is not a diagnosis: the cohorts show a clear advantage when leaving the weakest group, and strength can be trained.10

Do knee push-ups count?

They are good training but cannot be compared with the full push-up, because they carry less weight.14 No study I read gives a risk threshold for this variant.

And for women?

I did not find a study linking the number of push-ups in women to cardiac events. Hand strength predicts mortality in them as in men.8,9
